title: A Cipher for the Witness Anew
premise: When estate lawyer Kestrel Whitlock is called to probate a will naming the town's founder, Edmund Voss, as its testator—despite his burial thirty years ago—they assume it's a clerical fraud. But the exhumation reveals an empty coffin, and the will's terms threaten to dissolve the Voss family's grip on Harrowgate's land, water, and politics. As Kestrel digs into three 'accidental' deaths from 1994 that mirror the will's suspiciously precise bequests, they uncover that Edmund faked his death to escape his own family and hid the truth in a cipher only a witness he trusted could read. The statute of limitations expires in eleven days; Kestrel must decode the cipher, expose which Voss heir committed murder to protect the inheritance, and choose between turning in the one person who ever made them feel they belong—Edmund himself, alive and complicit—or letting duty bury love. In the end, Kestrel files the will, names the killer, and walks away from Harrowgate with Edmund's confession sealed and their own invisibility finally, deliberately surrendered.
about_author: Petra Okafor spent a decade as a probate paralegal in small-town New England before turning her case files into fiction. She writes mysteries about the paperwork people leave behind and the lives it quietly governs.

chapters.title: The Will That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Kestrel Whitlock, POV. A courier delivers a notarized will signed by Edmund Voss—dead for thirty years—with a probate date stamped next week. Kestrel, who has solved three deaths the police mislabeled, recognizes the handwriting quirks as genuine. The emotional beat: the thrill of an impossible puzzle colliding with dread, because whoever filed this wants something buried dug up.

chapters.title: Empty Oak
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV, with Detective Ilsa Reyes reluctantly present. The court orders exhumation; the coffin holds only a lead-lined box of river stones and a brass plate engraved with a nine-symbol cipher. Townsfolk gather at the cemetery fence, whispering. Emotional beat: public exposure—the invisible Kestrel suddenly watched by every eye in Harrowgate, belonging offered like a trap.

chapters.title: Heirs of the Hollow
chapters.summary: Kestrel interviews the Voss heirs: matriarch Cordelia, who runs the water company; grandson Tobias, a failing developer; and ward Marisol, who was a child in 1994. Each alibi for the night Edmund 'died' is polished, rehearsed, identical. Emotional beat: Kestrel's loneliness sharpening into resolve—these people perform family; Kestrel knows the difference.

chapters.title: Three Accidents, One Year
chapters.summary: Flashback interleave: Kestrel reviews their own past cases—the boathouse fall, the barn fire, the drowned surveyor—all 1994, all witnesses to something at Voss land. Reyes notices the pattern too and offers an uneasy alliance. Emotional beat: the cold recognition that Kestrel's quiet victories were never accidents of curiosity but threads of one larger crime.

chapters.title: The Cipher of Stones
chapters.summary: Kestrel decodes the brass plate using the founder's own survey ledgers: it maps to coordinates beneath the old mill and a message—'I am the witness anew.' At the mill they find Edmund's hidden study, journals, and evidence he staged his death to flee his family's crimes. Emotional beat: vertigo of sympathy—the victim may be the author of everything.

chapters.title: What Cordelia Kept
chapters.summary: Cordelia, POV. She confesses partially: she knew her father lived, has received letters for thirty years, and burned the ones naming who killed the three witnesses. Her chapter reveals the murders protected the inheritance scheme Tobias now revives. Emotional beat: a mother's power curdling into complicity—power corrupting even love.

chapters.title: Eleven Days
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV. The statute expires in eleven days; Tobias, sensing exposure, moves to have Kestrel disbarred on fabricated ethics charges and buys off the judge. Marisol secretly brings Kestrel a letter she found—one of Edmund's unburned ones. Emotional beat: siege pressure; Kestrel's duty to the law versus the growing pull toward the man behind the cipher.

chapters.title: The Witness Anew
chapters.summary: Kestrel follows the letter to a lakeside cabin and meets Edmund Voss, alive, aged, unrepentant about fleeing but shattered about the deaths. He admits he wrote the will to force the truth open after learning Tobias killed the witnesses—and that he named Kestrel executor because he'd watched them solve the other cases. Emotional beat: love against duty, fully ignited; Kestrel holding the confession that could save or destroy him.

chapters.title: Probate of Bones
chapters.summary: Climax. Kestrel convenes the probate hearing, presents the decoded cipher, the mill evidence, and Edmund's sworn statement. Tobias breaks when confronted with the surveyor's recovered watch; Cordelia turns on him to save what remains of the name. Reyes arrests Tobias as the gavel falls. Emotional beat: Kestrel choosing duty publicly while privately shielding Edmund's escape—corruption answered, love preserved in secret.

chapters.title: A Name Given Freely
chapters.summary: Resolution, Kestrel POV. Weeks later: the Voss holdings transfer to the town, Marisol rebuilds the water trust, and Kestrel declines a partnership offer to open a small practice taking cases no one else wants. On the last page, a postcard arrives unsigned—a lake, a single line of cipher reading 'thank you.' Emotional beat: belonging finally chosen, not inherited; invisibility traded for a self-made name.
